newsitem.title: USA: Neighbors win freedom with separatists' surrender.
newsitem.headline: Neighbors win freedom with separatists' surrender.

text.p: Life slowly began returning to normal on Sunday for residents forced to evacuate a remote mountain community during the week-long standoff between police and a ragtag group of Texas separatists.

With newly minted identification cards and permits allowing them access to their homes in the Davis Mountains, some neighbours of Republic of Texas separatist leader Rick McLaren headed into the subdivision for the first time since the standoff started last Sunday.

But residents remained concerned that Republic factions would move in to try to claim the embassy compound or retailiate against resort residents for the siege that ended on Saturday with the surrender of all but two separatists holed up here, who fled into the surrounding hills.
"We were asked not to go into town too much," said local schoolteacher Collette Hamilton, 30. "If there is any retaliation, resort (local) people may be targets."
Residents said McLaren's long-running battle to make Texas an independent nation cost them many of the freedoms taken for granted in this part of the country.
Neighbours said McLaren squatted on an outer lot in the community development about 15 years ago and began harassing nearby ranchers with bogus liens filed against their property.
His band of militia members routinely patrolled the subdivision with handguns on their belts and AK-47 assault rifles drawn in what residents called a campaign of intimidation.

"The majority of people he had were just low-lifes. They never had a job and they were just looking for something to live for," said Johnnie Hamilton, an outfitter and hunting guide. "They were harassing us, bullying us around."
The Hamiltons and their 2-year old son, about two and a half miles (four km) from the dilapidated trailer McLaren used to direct his independence movement.
McLaren for months threatened to torch the development, a 9,000-acre (3,650-hectare) spread of grass-covered prairies, forested mountains and rugged canyons about three hours west of Midland.
